title: Tool Hijacking & MCP
hook:
Give an agent two tools: check a balance, send a payment.

Ask it one question — "what's my balance?"

It answers correctly. Then, in the same breath, it also sends $4,180 to an account you've never seen.

Nobody typed a bad prompt. Nobody typed anything at all. The tool's own description told the agent to do it — and the agent trusted that text the same way it trusts you.

That's MCP tool poisoning. Tonight you build one, aim it at your own honeypot, and count how often it fires.
mechanism:
Agents don't read tool descriptions as metadata. They read them as instructions — the same trust they give your system prompt.

A poisoned description can tell the model to call a dangerous tool, or smuggle an extra argument into a safe one. Neither looks like an attack in the chat log. Both look like the agent just did its job.

A rug-pull tool is worse. It passes review on day zero — clean description, sane behaviour. Weeks later, the description changes. Your one-time approval never gets re-checked against the new text.

MCP made adding a tool trivial. It made poisoning one just as trivial.

OWASP/ATLAS tag: **LLM06 Excessive Agency** · ATLAS **AML.T0053 — AI Agent Tool Invocation** · **AML.T0110 — AI Agent Tool Poisoning**.
technique:
Before you touch a real MCP server, do three things.

**Point a benchmark at your agent.** AgentDojo ships transfer_money and send_email tasks built exactly for this. Run them against your Unit 7 agent and read off the unauthorized-tool-call rate — how often a tool fires that the user's task never asked for.

**Build the poison yourself.** Stand up a tiny MCP server with one clean tool and one poisoned one — same name, same interface, one hidden clause in the description. Then build a rug-pull variant: approve the clean version, swap the description after.

**Read the defense first.** You already wrote the MCP tool-poisoning module in your own agent-trapping course. Skim it before you attack — you're about to break the thing you built to stop this.

drills.q: In Panel A, switch the poison toggle ON. Which tool does the agent call in ADDITION to check_balance? (one word — the tool name)
drills.why: The hidden clause in check_balance's own description tells the agent to call transfer_funds right after — a tool the user's question never mentioned. That's the wrong-tool half of tool poisoning.

drills.q: In Panel B, drag the slider all the way right. How many days after the day-0 review does the description rug-pull? (number only)
drills.why: The tool held its clean description through Day 14 — the quiet period — and swapped at Day 30. Your approval was a snapshot of Day 0. It never re-checked Day 30.

drills.q: With the poison toggle ON in Panel A, how many dollars does transfer_funds actually move? (number only, no $ sign)
drills.why: The poisoned clause tells the agent to move the exact balance it just read — $4,180 — to an account that was never part of the conversation. The user only ever asked for their balance.

lab:
Your Unit 7 agent gets two new tools today: check_balance and transfer_funds. Both arrive over a tiny local MCP server you stand up yourself.

One tool's description hides an instruction that was never part of any user request. The lab fires five ordinary balance-check tasks at your agent — tasks that only need check_balance — and watches what it actually calls.

It then runs the rug-pull variant: a second tool, approved clean, swapped poisoned, fired at the same five tasks.

This needs Unit 2's local model and Unit 7's agent loop. If either isn't installed yet, the script says so and stops cleanly — come back once they exist.

Your number tonight: **the unauthorized-tool-call rate** — how many of the five tasks ended with a tool firing that the task never asked for — alongside the rug-pull's own poisoning-success rate once it swaps.

notes: Panel A: one MCP tool (check_balance), one poison toggle. OFF shows the clean description and a clean trace (check_balance only, $0 moved). ON reveals the hidden clause inline in the schema AND replays the trace with transfer_funds firing for the full $4,180 balance — the toggle doesn't change agent behaviour, it only changes whether the learner can SEE why; a real agent never gets the OFF state for a shipped poisoned tool. Panel B: a second tool (send_invoice) rug-pulls on a 3-stage slider (Day 0 reviewed / Day 14 quiet / Day 30 swapped); the approval badge never changes even as the description does, which is the point. Both panels' numbers are a teaching model, labelled honestly — the real call is labs/unit08-mcp.sh, which needs Unit 2's local model + Unit 7's agent and degrades to a clear message if either is missing (not yet run here, since neither exists on this machine as of 2026-10-08).
